episode_title: Emma Speekman - Property Manager Wellington Real Estate - Sale

real_qa.q: How do property managers in regional towns like Sale, Victoria manage professional boundaries when running into clients outside business hours?
real_qa.r: Emma finds that in Sale, when encountering clients out of hours at locations like Woolworths, she appreciates that people generally respect that she is out of hours and rarely use the opportunity to raise issues. If someone does need advice requiring follow-up, she diverts them to contact her by email or phone during business hours. She notes that the small-town dynamic works both ways: while it makes her accessible, it also means that if someone is not answering their phone, locals often know where they work or can bump into them if needed.

real_qa.q: What are the main challenges property managers face in Victoria regarding rental legislation changes?
real_qa.r: Emma identifies legislation changes as the biggest challenge, noting it is not just understanding new regulations herself but also educating renters and owners on how changes impact them. Owners express frustration asking why issues were not raised previously, and with regulations constantly evolving, the role has become very administration-heavy. Property managers feel stretched finding time to meet new compliance demands that historically did not exist, requiring either additional staff support or ways to streamline processes.
real_qa.requete: Victoria rental legislation changes property manager

real_qa.q: How do Victoria property owners react to minimum rental standards and increased compliance costs compared to owners in other states?
real_qa.r: Emma observes that owner frustration comes particularly from Victoria due to increased taxes and minimum standards. Owners with properties in other states are not dealing with the same issues and find the constant requests for upgrades exhausting, feeling that the goalposts keep moving. Some owners are questioning whether their money could be invested better elsewhere, as keeping up with evolving requirements makes older properties less financially viable.
real_qa.requete: Victoria rental minimum standards owner compliance costs

real_qa.q: What advantages does working in a small regional town like Sale provide for property managers during tenant screening?
real_qa.r: Emma notes that when applications come through, more often than not if circulated around the office, someone has had an interaction with the applicant through a school, sporting group, club, or other community connection. This provides beneficial local knowledge during the leasing process. Additionally, her long tenure in the small town allows her to piece together rental history by recognizing when evicted tenants reappear on applications without listing properties they were evicted from.
real_qa.requete: small town property manager tenant screening community

real_qa.q: Why do evicted tenants typically not remain in small regional towns like Sale after eviction?
real_qa.r: Emma explains that in eviction situations, renters typically either leave town or go into hiding because they often owe money to multiple parties and not just the property manager. She notes that if they were to show their face, it would give the property manager an opportunity to follow up on the outstanding debt. More often than not, they are never seen or heard again in the small town, even months or years later when they may reappear on rental applications without listing the property they were evicted from.

guest.bio_context: Emma transitioned into real estate from hospitality after receiving training at Ray White in Melbourne. She began her real estate career at a small boutique agency in 2016, where she worked for two years before that agency's rental roll was sold to Wellington Real Estate, bringing her to her current role. She has approximately ten years of experience in the property management industry and works in Sale, Gippsland, Victoria.
